claim: TAF4 is expressed in P12 wild-type hepatocytes, mesenchymal tissues, endothelial and smooth muscle cells around the hepatic veins and arteries, and cholangiocytes lining the bile ducts.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed TAF4 expression in P12 wild-type (WT) hepatocytes, mesenchymal tissues, endothelial and smooth muscle cells around the hepatic veins and arteries, and cholangiocytes lining the bile ducts (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: TAF4 and TBP are expressed in late embryonic hepatocytes.
source: TAF4 and TBP are expressed in late embryonic hepatocytes and TBP remains strongly expressed in adult hepatocytes, while TAF4 expression is reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TBP remains strongly expressed in adult hepatocytes, while TAF4 expression is reduced.
source: TAF4 and TBP are expressed in late embryonic hepatocytes and TBP remains strongly expressed in adult hepatocytes, while TAF4 expression is reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAF4 and TBP are expressed from the embryonic to adult stages, with high expression in neonatal liver.
source: TAF4 and TBP are therefore expressed from the embryonic to adult stages, with high expression in neonatal liver.
evidence: Inferred from the expression patterns described in the text and supported by immunostaining data.

claim: Reduced TAF4 expression in adult hepatocytes has been previously reported.
source: Reduced TAF4 expression in adult hepatocytes has been previously reported (D'Alessio et al., 2011), but we do not observe the reported strong loss of TBP expression.
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Alessio et al., 2011.

claim: The authors do not observe the reported strong loss of TBP expression in adult hepatocytes.
source: Reduced TAF4 expression in adult hepatocytes has been previously reported (D'Alessio et al., 2011), but we do not observe the reported strong loss of TBP expression.
evidence: Supported by the authors' own observations contrasting with previous reports.

claim: TAF4 expression is lost from hepatocytes by P12 in Taf4ahep−/− mice.
source: TAF4 expression is lost from hepatocytes by P12 (Figure 1A–B), although it remains in the portal vein mesenchyme, endothelial cells, cholangiocytes of extra-hepatic bile ducts, and bile ducts close to the liver hilum, but not in cholangiocytes forming peripheral bile ducts (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: TAF4 remains expressed in the portal vein mesenchyme, endothelial cells, cholangiocytes of extra-hepatic bile ducts, and bile ducts close to the liver hilum in Taf4ahep−/− mice.
source: TAF4 expression is lost from hepatocytes by P12 (Figure 1A–B), although it remains in the portal vein mesenchyme, endothelial cells, cholangiocytes of extra-hepatic bile ducts, and bile ducts close to the liver hilum, but not in cholangiocytes forming peripheral bile ducts (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: TAF4 is not expressed in cholangiocytes forming peripheral bile ducts in Taf4ahep−/− mice.
source: TAF4 expression is lost from hepatocytes by P12 (Figure 1A–B), although it remains in the portal vein mesenchyme, endothelial cells, cholangiocytes of extra-hepatic bile ducts, and bile ducts close to the liver hilum, but not in cholangiocytes forming peripheral bile ducts (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: Taf4ahep−/− animals are born at Mendelian ratios.
source: Taf4ahep−/− animals are born at Mendelian ratios and no prenatal abnormalities or lethality were observed (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study.

claim: No prenatal abnormalities or lethality were observed in Taf4ahep−/− animals.
source: Taf4ahep−/− animals are born at Mendelian ratios and no prenatal abnormalities or lethality were observed (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Taf4ahep−/− animals are of normal weight and size at birth.
source: Taf4ahep−/− animals are of normal weight and size at birth, show retarded growth by P12, begin to die between P12 and P14, and all are dead by P21 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements and observations shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Taf4ahep−/− animals show retarded growth by P12.
source: Taf4ahep−/− animals are of normal weight and size at birth, show retarded growth by P12, begin to die between P12 and P14, and all are dead by P21 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements and observations shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Taf4ahep−/− animals begin to die between P12 and P14.
source: Taf4ahep−/− animals are of normal weight and size at birth, show retarded growth by P12, begin to die between P12 and P14, and all are dead by P21 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: All Taf4ahep−/− animals are dead by P21.
source: Taf4ahep−/− animals are of normal weight and size at birth, show retarded growth by P12, begin to die between P12 and P14, and all are dead by P21 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Taf4ahep−/− animals display severe physiological and morphological alterations caused by perturbed liver function.
source: Mutants display severe physiological and morphological alterations caused by perturbed liver function.
evidence: Inferred from the observed phenotypes described in the manuscript.

claim: Cholestatic lesions of mutant livers were evident at P2 with marked jaundice of the animals.
source: Cholestatic lesions of mutant livers were evident at P2 with marked jaundice of the animals whose severity rapidly increases over the next days (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: Supported by observations and images shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: The severity of jaundice rapidly increases over the days following P2 in Taf4ahep−/− animals.
source: Cholestatic lesions of mutant livers were evident at P2 with marked jaundice of the animals whose severity rapidly increases over the next days (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: Supported by observations and images shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: By P12, Taf4ahep−/− animals display 50% reduced body weight and severe jaundice.
source: By P12, knockout animals display 50% reduced body weight and severe jaundice (Figure 2A,B) and their livers become completely yellow with visible patches of bile deposits within the parenchyma (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements and observations shown in Figure 2A,B,C.

claim: By P12, the livers of Taf4ahep−/− animals become completely yellow with visible patches of bile deposits within the parenchyma.
source: By P12, knockout animals display 50% reduced body weight and severe jaundice (Figure 2A,B) and their livers become completely yellow with visible patches of bile deposits within the parenchyma (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by observations and images shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Taf4ahep−/− mice display severe hypoglycemia with glucose levels below 3.0 mmol/l in both males and females.
source: Blood plasma analysis revealed severe hypoglycemia in Taf4ahep−/− mice with glucose levels below 3.0 mmol/l in both males and females that is the most probable cause of early lethality (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by blood plasma analysis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Severe hypoglycemia is the most probable cause of early lethality in Taf4ahep−/− mice.
source: Blood plasma analysis revealed severe hypoglycemia in Taf4ahep−/− mice with glucose levels below 3.0 mmol/l in both males and females that is the most probable cause of early lethality (Figure 2D).
evidence: Inferred from the severe hypoglycemia observed in the mutant mice.

claim: High levels of bile acids and bilirubin were detected in the plasma of Taf4ahep−/− mice.
source: In accordance with their jaundiced appearance, we also detected high levels of bile acids and bilirubin in the plasma of the Taf4ahep−/− mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by blood plasma analysis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The levels of free fatty acids (FFA), triglycerides (TA), and total cholesterol do not significantly change in Taf4ahep−/− mice compared to WT mice.
source: In contrast, the levels of free fatty acids (FFA), triglycerides (TA), and total cholesterol do not significantly change, but HDL cholesterol is considerably reduced compared to WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by blood plasma analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HDL cholesterol is considerably reduced in Taf4ahep−/− mice compared to WT mice.
source: In contrast, the levels of free fatty acids (FFA), triglycerides (TA), and total cholesterol do not significantly change, but HDL cholesterol is considerably reduced compared to WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by blood plasma analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAF4 knockout in post-natal hepatocytes causes severe liver malfunction, hypoglycemia, and dysfunctional bile and lipid transport and metabolism.
source: TAF4 knockout in post-natal hepatocytes therefore causes severe liver malfunction, hypoglycemia, and dysfunctional bile and lipid transport and metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple phenotypes observed in the mutant mice.

claim: TAF4 mutant livers display alterations in parenchyma and lobule organisation with disorganised hepatocyte disposition in lobules and non-aligned hepatic plates due to variations in cell size.
source: TAF4 mutant livers display alterations in parenchyma and lobule organisation with disorganised hepatocyte disposition in lobules and non-aligned hepatic plates due to variations in cell size (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Periportal hepatocytes in TAF4 mutant livers are markedly vacuolated and often display foamy intra-cytoplasmic inclusions indicating steatosis.
source: Periportal hepatocytes are markedly vacuolated and often display foamy intra-cytoplasmic inclusions indicating steatosis (white arrows in Figure 2E, oil red staining in Figure 2F–G).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and oil red staining shown in Figure 2E, F, G.

claim: PAS staining revealed a lack of glycogen in TAF4 knockouts.
source: PAS staining revealed a lack of glycogen in TAF4 knockouts (Figure 2F), which along with hypoglycemia shows defective carbohydrate metabolism in Tafa4hep−/− mice.
evidence: Supported by PAS staining shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The lack of glycogen along with hypoglycemia shows defective carbohydrate metabolism in Taf4ahep−/− mice.
source: PAS staining revealed a lack of glycogen in TAF4 knockouts (Figure 2F), which along with hypoglycemia shows defective carbohydrate metabolism in Tafa4hep−/− mice.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of glycogen and hypoglycemia observed in the mutant mice.

claim: Large and bi-nucleate hepatocytes were observed mostly in pericentral areas of TAF4 mutant livers.
source: We also observed large and bi-nucleate hepatocytes mostly in pericentral areas, many necrotic cells in periportal regions (Figure 2G), and a dramatic reduction in proliferating KI67 positive hepatocytes (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Many necrotic cells were observed in periportal regions of TAF4 mutant livers.
source: We also observed large and bi-nucleate hepatocytes mostly in pericentral areas, many necrotic cells in periportal regions (Figure 2G), and a dramatic reduction in proliferating KI67 positive hepatocytes (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A dramatic reduction in proliferating KI67 positive hepatocytes was observed in TAF4 mutant livers.
source: We also observed large and bi-nucleate hepatocytes mostly in pericentral areas, many necrotic cells in periportal regions (Figure 2G), and a dramatic reduction in proliferating KI67 positive hepatocytes (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by KI67 immunostaining shown in Figure 2H.

claim: In WT P5 liver, bile ducts were seen in both the hilum and peripheral regions.
source: In WT P5 liver, bile ducts were seen in both the hilum and peripheral regions (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Taf4ahep−/− liver, bile ducts with a clear lumen were formed in the hilum, but their number rapidly decreases towards the periphery.
source: In Taf4ahep−/− liver, bile ducts with a clear lumen were formed in the hilum, but their number rapidly decreases towards to periphery where residual cholangiocytes organised as bi-layered ductal structures that fail to undergo normal tubulogenesis (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Residual cholangiocytes in the periphery of Taf4ahep−/− liver are organised as bi-layered ductal structures that fail to undergo normal tubulogenesis.
source: In Taf4ahep−/− liver, bile ducts with a clear lumen were formed in the hilum, but their number rapidly decreases towards to periphery where residual cholangiocytes organised as bi-layered ductal structures that fail to undergo normal tubulogenesis (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Staining cholangiocytes at P12 with SOX9 showed normally formed mesenchyme-integrated bile ducts in the periportal regions of the hilum and periphery in WT liver.
source: Staining cholangiocytes at P12 with SOX9 showed normally formed mesenchyme-integrated bile ducts in the periportal regions of the hilum and periphery in WT liver (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Staining for CLDN3 marking the apical pole of the ductal cells revealed properly formed ducts with a clear lumen in WT liver.
source: Staining for CLDN3 marking the apical pole of the ductal cells revealed properly formed ducts with a clear lumen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In mutant liver, SOX9 positive cholangiocytes were observed, but even when located next to the large portal vein towards the hilum they did not form tubular ducts.
source: In mutant liver, SOX9 positive cholangiocytes were also observed, but even when located next to the large portal vein towards the hilum they did not form tubular ducts (Figure 3B) although CLDN3 staining revealed cell polarisation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CLDN3 staining revealed cell polarisation in mutant liver cholangiocytes.
source: In mutant liver, SOX9 positive cholangiocytes were also observed, but even when located next to the large portal vein towards the hilum they did not form tubular ducts (Figure 3B) although CLDN3 staining revealed cell polarisation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Staining with ACTA2 showed hepatic arteries adjacent to normal bile ducts in WT liver, which were absent in the peripheral regions of Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: Staining with ACTA2 showed hepatic arteries adjacent to normal bile ducts in WT liver, which were absent in the peripheral regions of Taf4ahep−/− liver (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Portal vein mesenchyme was significantly reduced in mutant liver.
source: Portal vein mesenchyme was also significantly reduced in mutant liver (Figures 3B and 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3B and 1A.

claim: Electron microscopy confirmed proper formation of bile ducts with lumen in WT liver, but disorganised ducts without lumen in Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: Electron microscopy confirmed proper formation of bile ducts with lumen in WT liver, but disorganised ducts without lumen in Taf4ahep−/− liver (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The presence of ducts in the hilar region and their absence in the peripheral regions suggest that maturation is normally initiated during embryogenesis but is arrested upon TAF4 inactivation.
source: The presence of ducts in the hilar region and their absence in the peripheral regions suggest that maturation is normally initiated during embryogenesis but is arrested upon TAF4 inactivation.
evidence: Inferred from the spatial distribution of bile duct formation in the mutant liver.

claim: The TAF4 knockout phenotype is similar to the loss of Notch signalling, associated with Alagille syndrome in humans.
source: The above phenotype is similar to the loss of Notch signalling, associated with Alagille syndrome in humans, essential for normal bile duct numbers and morphogenesis (Zong et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison with known phenotypes from the literature, supported by citation to Zong et al., 2009.

claim: Notch signalling is essential for normal bile duct numbers and morphogenesis.
source: The above phenotype is similar to the loss of Notch signalling, associated with Alagille syndrome in humans, essential for normal bile duct numbers and morphogenesis (Zong et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zong et al., 2009.

claim: TAF4 may act as a cofactor for transcription factors of the Notch signalling pathway.
source: These similarities suggest that TAF4 may act as a cofactor for transcription factors of the Notch signalling pathway.
evidence: Speculative inference based on phenotypic similarities.

claim: The under-development of portal vein mesenchyme and hepatic arteries associated with defective bile duct morphogenesis supports the reported reciprocal nature of biliary, vascular, and mesenchyme maturation.
source: In addition, the under-development of portal vein mesenchyme and hepatic arteries associated with defective bile duct morphogenesis supports the reported reciprocal nature of biliary, vascular, and mesenchyme maturation (Hofmann et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by observations in the study and citation to Hofmann et al., 2010.

claim: Taf4ahep−/− liver displayed abnormal spaces between hepatocyte membranes indicative of impaired cell contacts and reduced number of tight junctions.
source: Taf4ahep−/− liver displayed abnormal spaces between hepatocyte membranes indicative of impaired cell contacts and reduced number of tight junctions (Figure 2G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CLDN3 and TJP1 staining showed extensive tight junctions all around the membrane of wild-type hepatocytes.
source: CLDN3 and TJP1 staining showed extensive tight junctions all around the membrane of wild-type hepatocytes, whereas, in the Taf4ahep−/− hepatocytes, staining was irregular and patchy, and many cells showed little or no staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: In Taf4ahep−/− hepatocytes, CLDN3 and TJP1 staining was irregular and patchy, and many cells showed little or no staining.
source: CLDN3 and TJP1 staining showed extensive tight junctions all around the membrane of wild-type hepatocytes, whereas, in the Taf4ahep−/− hepatocytes, staining was irregular and patchy, and many cells showed little or no staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Impaired cell–cell contacts and the absence of tubular bile ducts account for the observed accumulation of bile in the liver parenchyma and in the blood of the mutant animals.
source: Consequently, impaired cell–cell contacts and the absence of tubular bile ducts account for the observed accumulation of bile in the liver parenchyma and in the blood of the mutant animals.
evidence: Inferred from the observed defects in cell junctions and bile duct formation.

claim: In TAF4-mutant liver, 1408 genes were down-regulated and 776 up-regulated compared to wild-type.
source: In TAF4-mutant liver, 1408 genes were down-regulated and 776 up-regulated compared to wild-type (Figure 4A, and Figure 4A—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1, [Alpern et al., 2014])
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A and supplementary files.

claim: The changes in expression of a selected set of genes were confirmed by RT-qPCR.
source: The changes in expression of a selected set of genes were confirmed by RT-qPCR (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Down-regulated genes are predominately expressed in liver (endoderm).
source: Down-regulated genes are predominately expressed in liver (endoderm), whereas the majority of up-regulated genes are annotated as enriched in brain, nervous system, and testis (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ontology analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The majority of up-regulated genes are annotated as enriched in brain, nervous system, and testis.
source: Down-regulated genes are predominately expressed in liver (endoderm), whereas the majority of up-regulated genes are annotated as enriched in brain, nervous system, and testis (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ontology analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Around 50% of down-regulated genes clustered with those showing low embryonic expression and induction by P7.
source: Around 50% of down-regulated genes clustered with those showing low embryonic expression and induction by P7 (Figure 4C, clusters 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Up-regulated genes are most represented amongst genes whose expression is high at E18.5 and down-regulated between P7 and P14.
source: In contrast and despite the fact that only a minority of up-regulated transcripts were present in the Li et al. data, they are most represented amongst genes whose expression is high at E18.5 and down-regulated between P7 and P14 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The mean expression of down-regulated genes increased after birth in WT.
source: The mean expression of down-regulated genes increased after birth in WT, whereas that of the up-regulated genes decreased (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The mean expression of up-regulated genes decreased after birth in WT.
source: The mean expression of down-regulated genes increased after birth in WT, whereas that of the up-regulated genes decreased (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Several imprinted genes were up-regulated in mutant liver.
source: Interestingly, several imprinted genes (Dlk1, Meg3, Dio3, Plagl1, Peg3, Peg10, Igf2as, Airn, Igf2r, Malat1, Neat1, and Grb10) were up-regulated in mutant liver.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Imprinted genes regulate fetal growth and are post-natal repressed.
source: These genes regulate fetal growth and are post-natal repressed.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about imprinted genes.

claim: Expression of imprinted genes is a hallmark of immature tissue.
source: Expression of these genes is a hallmark of immature tissue, showing that TAF4 is required for normal post-natal hepatoblast maturation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about imprinted genes and inference from the data.

claim: TAF4 is required for normal post-natal hepatoblast maturation.
source: Expression of these genes is a hallmark of immature tissue, showing that TAF4 is required for normal post-natal hepatoblast maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the expression of imprinted genes in the mutant.

claim: TAF4 expression was strongly decreased in extracts from P12 Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: TAF4 expression was strongly decreased in extracts from P12 Taf4ahep−/− liver (Figure 5A) but not totally lost since its expression persisted in the non-hepatocyte cells of the liver.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: TAF4 expression was not totally lost in Taf4ahep−/− liver since its expression persisted in the non-hepatocyte cells of the liver.
source: TAF4 expression was strongly decreased in extracts from P12 Taf4ahep−/− liver (Figure 5A) but not totally lost since its expression persisted in the non-hepatocyte cells of the liver.
evidence: Inferred from the Western blot data and knowledge of cell-type specific expression.

claim: Expression of TBP and several TAFs was diminished in Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: Expression of TBP and several TAFs was also diminished while little change was observed for TFIIB, TFIIE, Pol II, and HNF4A (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Little change was observed for TFIIB, TFIIE, Pol II, and HNF4A expression in Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: Expression of TBP and several TAFs was also diminished while little change was observed for TFIIB, TFIIE, Pol II, and HNF4A (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Diminished amounts of all tested TAFs were observed in the TBP IP from Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: We performed anti-TBP immunoprecipitation (IP) and normalised the amount of IP TBP from WT and Taf4ahep−/− liver. Under these conditions, diminished amounts of all tested TAFs were observed in the TBP IP from Taf4ahep−/− (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss of TAF4 led to reduced TBP and TAF accumulation likely due to the disassembly of TFIID witnessed by the reduced co-precipitation of TAFs with TBP.
source: Thus, consistent with the critical role of TAF4 in the TFIID core complex (Wright et al., 2006, Bieniossek et al., 2013), loss of TAF4 led to reduced TBP and TAF accumulation likely due to the disassembly of TFIID witnessed by the reduced co-precipitation of TAFs with TBP.
evidence: Inferred from the immunoprecipitation data and supported by citations to Wright et al., 2006 and Bieniossek et al., 2013.

claim: No significant expression of TAF4b was seen in extracts from WT and Taf4ahep−/− liver and in the respective TBP IPs.
source: No significant expression of TAF4b that can replace TAF4 in the core complex was seen in extracts from WT and Taf4ahep−/− liver and in the respective TBP IPs (Figure 5D and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: TAF4b cannot substitute for TAF4 to maintain TFIID integrity in liver tissue.
source: TAF4b therefore cannot substitute for TAF4 to maintain TFIID integrity in this tissue.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of TAF4b expression in the liver.

claim: The TBP, TFIIB, and TFIIE ChIP-seq data indicated a global decrease in their genomic occupancy and a 2–2.5 fold lower occupancy at the TSS of expressed genes in Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: The TBP, TFIIB, and TFIIE ChIP-seq data indicated a global decrease in their genomic occupancy and a 2–2.5 fold lower occupancy at the TSS of expressed genes in Taf4ahep−/− liver (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No comparable decrease in CTCF occupancy was seen in Taf4ahep−/− liver, and its distribution is largely unchanged.
source: No comparable decrease was seen for CTCF whose distribution is largely unchanged (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A much stronger decrease in PIC formation was seen at the TSS of down-regulated genes.
source: A much stronger decrease in PIC formation was seen at the TSS of down-regulated genes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: An almost two-fold reduction of promoter-proximal paused and elongating Pol II was seen at all expressed genes, with a much stronger reduction at down-regulated genes.
source: Similarly, an almost two-fold reduction of promoter-proximal paused and elongating Pol II was seen at all expressed genes, with a much stronger reduction at down-regulated genes (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PIC formation, Pol II recruitment, and H3K4me3 were lost at the TSS of Dio1 in Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: For example, PIC formation, Pol II recruitment, and H3K4me3 were lost at the TSS of Dio1 that is post-natal induced in WT (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Loss of expression of post-natal activated liver function genes in Taf4ahep−/− liver corresponds to defective PIC formation in the absence of TAF4.
source: Similar results were seen at many other post-natal activated liver function genes indicating that loss of their expression in Taf4ahep−/− liver corresponds to defective PIC formation in the absence of TAF4.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Diminished PIC formation was observed at up-regulated genes with reduced paused Pol II downstream of the TSS.
source: More intriguingly, diminished PIC formation was also observed at up-regulated genes with reduced paused Pol II downstream of the TSS (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The Pol II meta-profile shows that levels of elongating Pol II were comparable in WT and mutant, indicating reduced Pol II pausing and a relative increase in elongating Pol II in Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: The Pol II meta-profile shows, however, that levels of elongating Pol II were comparable in WT and mutant indicating reduced Pol II pausing and a relative increase in elongating Pol II in Taf4ahep−/− liver.
evidence: Inferred from the Pol II ChIP-seq meta-profile analysis.

claim: At the Angptl4 gene, equivalent amounts of PIC and paused Pol II were seen in WT and mutant, whereas a higher density of elongating Pol II was observed in Taf4ahep−/− liver.
source: This is exemplified at the Angptl4 gene where equivalent amounts of PIC and paused Pol II were seen in WT and mutant, whereas a higher density of elongating Pol II was observed in Taf4ahep−/− liver (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ChIP-qPCR indicated enhanced recruitment of the CDK9 subunit of PTEFb at the TSS, gene body, and 3′UTR of the Angptl4, Malat, and Ehhadh genes in the mutant.
source: ChIP-qPCR indicated enhanced recruitment of the CDK9 subunit of the positive regulator of elongation PTEFb at the TSS, gene body, and 3′UTR of the Angptl4, Malat, and Ehhadh genes in the mutant, whereas no such increase was seen at down-regulated genes that displayed a generally low level of CDK9 (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: No increase in CDK9 recruitment was seen at down-regulated genes that displayed a generally low level of CDK9.
source: ChIP-qPCR indicated enhanced recruitment of the CDK9 subunit of the positive regulator of elongation PTEFb at the TSS, gene body, and 3′UTR of the Angptl4, Malat, and Ehhadh genes in the mutant, whereas no such increase was seen at down-regulated genes that displayed a generally low level of CDK9 (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: TAF4 regulates hepatocyte gene expression by controlling HNF4A occupancy, PIC formation, and Pol II pausing.
source: These results reveal two distinct mechanisms for gene regulation in Taf4ahep−/− liver. Down-regulation is due to defective PIC formation, while up-regulation of many genes reflects decreased pausing and increased elongating Pol II and CDK9 recruitment.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Down-regulation of genes in Taf4ahep−/− liver is due to defective PIC formation.
source: These results reveal two distinct mechanisms for gene regulation in Taf4ahep−/− liver. Down-regulation is due to defective PIC formation, while up-regulation of many genes reflects decreased pausing and increased elongating Pol II and CDK9 recruitment.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Up-regulation of many genes in Taf4ahep−/− liver reflects decreased pausing and increased elongating Pol II and CDK9 recruitment.
source: These results reveal two distinct mechanisms for gene regulation in Taf4ahep−/− liver. Down-regulation is due to defective PIC formation, while up-regulation of many genes reflects decreased pausing and increased elongating Pol II and CDK9 recruitment.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: TAF3 was recruited to the TSS as expected for a TFIID component.
source: TAF3 was recruited to the TSS as expected for a TFIID component, but TAF3 occupancy and the levels of H3K4me3 at the TSS were much less affected than TBP occupancy and PIC formation (Figure 6A).
